subjects.question: Does evidence for drought explain a political ending?
subjects.summary: Hattusha was a place of government, worship, building and provisioning before it became a problem of collapse. Its royal administration depended on people moving food and maintaining institutions across a changing city. Evidence for severe drought near the political transformation adds a possible stress to that history. It does not turn the end of the central administration into the disappearance of everyone in the region.

sections.title: A capital coordinated more than royal display
sections.text: The DAI describes a capital and cult centre with a palace, temples and cuneiform archives. These institutions coordinated decisions, ritual obligations and resources. Maintaining their buildings required recurring work and supplies, connecting royal authority with builders and providers. The broad c. 1650–1180 BCE capital orientation is separate from this dossier’s 13th-century case. It does not describe the settlement’s whole lifespan or an unchanging arrangement of districts.

sections.text: Excavation in the northern Lower City traces residential construction from the earlier kārum period into Hittite phases and identifies housing alongside an official building. Schachner’s later synthesis describes settled areas moving and changing intensity through time. Dense districts could stand beside older ruins or open ground. A combined site plan is therefore a record assembled from different phases. It should not be read as a complete map of all the people, streets and buildings operating on the day the central government withdrew.

sections.title: Food could be stored, but resilience had limits
sections.text: The drought study discusses cereals as a food and tax base, with storage helping communities manage variable harvests. Repeated shortages pose a different problem from one bad season: using stored food leaves less protection if another crop fails. This is a proposed mechanism linking environmental stress to provisioning and political vulnerability. It is not a calculation of the grain left in every household or proof that all districts lacked alternatives. Distribution, access and decisions still matter when interpreting a material shortfall.

sections.title: The tree record has its own location and clock
sections.text: Manning and colleagues analyzed juniper timbers recovered at Gordion, about 230 km west of Hattusha. Ring widths and carbon isotopes indicate moisture conditions, rather than directly measuring decisions at the capital. They identify a severe dry episode around 1198–1196 BCE, with a ±3-year dating uncertainty. The central estimate falls just after the case endpoint of about 1200 BCE. The dating uncertainty can overlap that endpoint, so the wider reference frame shows the episode with its own dates. The authors acknowledge that direct causation remains unproved; abandonment of the royal centre also needs to be distinguished from later burning.

deeperReading.title: Separate a withdrawal from an empty landscape

The drought paper distinguishes the emptied royal centre and later burning, and discusses continuation and adaptation elsewhere in former Hittite territories. Schachner’s archaeological abstract offers another reason to resist a single dramatic snapshot: Hattusha’s occupied areas had changed long before the final political transition. A next investigation should ask which buildings stopped functioning, which activities moved and which evidence dates each change. The end of a document series is a consequential institutional event, but not a census proving that every resident left at once.

A plausible causal account must connect this regional stress with dated provisioning, institutions and human decisions. subjects.question: What traveled together on one ship?
subjects.summary: The Uluburun wreck preserves a shipment and traces of the people and skills that kept a ship working. Copper, tin, containers and valuable goods occurred together near the Anatolian coast. That association is secure evidence of movement, but recovering objects is different from identifying their ore sources, owners or destinations. The findspot, cargo and proposed origins need different visual and verbal labels.

A shipment thus joins production, packing, transport and exchange rather than representing one self-contained craft. The excavators’ date, c. 1320 BCE ±15 years, remains an approximate wreck window. Neither that window nor a mixed cargo identifies every port visited, the intended buyer or the political arrangement behind the voyage.

Such details bring building and maintenance into view beside the prestige goods. They do not provide a complete workday or a roster of specialists. Personal effects can support proposals about people aboard, but a vessel style or weapon should not become a certain nationality or a named passenger.

sections.title: A late capital is not the whole dynasty

Yin Xu, near Anyang, is a selected late capital dated by UNESCO to c. 1300–1046 BCE, with palace and ancestral shrine remains, royal tombs and inscribed bones. Its monumental and burial evidence concentrates attention on powerful institutions. It also includes pits with human remains interpreted as sacrificial victims. Authority involved unequal power and coercion as well as ceremony; the surviving elite record should not stand for an equal share in that power for every resident.

deeperReading.title: From a sample to an estimate

Analysts then grouped evidence by construction phase and location to identify concentrations consistent with buildings. This is a chain of interpretation, not a photograph of every occupied house. A floor may survive without its entire room, and a group of sampled floors still needs a defensible explanation. Estimating inhabitants adds another step: the 2020 study discusses an analogy with households in the local modern community of Tenochtitlán and explicitly acknowledges that ancient and present domestic groups are different. An estimate therefore joins archaeological observations to assumptions about how people shared space.

subjects.question: What work turned a sea crossing into a lasting island community?
subjects.summary: Potters, navigators and food producers helped establish communities across different island environments. Stamped designs, raw materials, dated tools and food evidence reveal different parts of that work. Their histories continued when decorated pottery changed; a shared pattern is a starting point for investigation, rather than a recovered voyage.

sections.title: A repeated mark became a larger design
sections.text: Lapita decoration began with practical actions. A potter pressed a toothed tool into clay before firing, combining small impressions into repeated bands and more elaborate figures. The Met describes vessels that may have cooked, served or stored food. Making such an object joined a useful container with choices about its surface. Repetition required control of spacing and direction: a pattern was something a maker constructed, rather than a label that appeared automatically on every pot.

sections.title: Settlement joined voyaging with provisioning
sections.text: Irwin’s regional account places the Lapita complex in the Bismarck Archipelago around 1500 BCE and movement toward Fiji and West Polynesia especially around 1100–800 BCE. These were different communities and stages, not one arrival everywhere. Coastal settings offered access to boats and marine resources. Transporting useful plants and animals could help establish livelihoods, while catching and gathering food sustained people locally. The timing and combination differed: the earliest eastern communities cannot simply be assigned an identical, fully established farming package.

sections.title: Potters also worked with local materials
sections.text: A shared decorative tradition did not require every vessel to arrive by canoe. Dickinson and Nunn examined sand temper in pottery from Fiji’s Rove Peninsula. Most sampled sherds used related local sands; a few contained nonlocal volcanic material. The authors interpret the latter as ceramic transfer. Distinguish that interpretation from the observed temper: identifying nonlocal material does not by itself rule out movement of raw ingredients or name a carrier. Looking inside the fabric changes the question from whether two designs resemble each other to how particular materials and finished objects may have moved.

sections.title: Meals made an island habitable
sections.text: At Teouma on Efate, researchers investigated dietary protein through bone-collagen isotopes and local food baselines. Their interpretation combines reef and inshore resources, wild terrestrial animals and domestic animals. This makes food acquisition and animal care part of settlement history, alongside navigation. It does not supply a complete menu: low-protein plant foods can be less visible in this kind of measurement. The study concerns one early Vanuatu community and must retain that setting when compared with other islands.

sections.title: Changing pottery did not end community history
sections.text: Tonga’s sequence shows why the pottery frame needs a longer context. Decorated vessels gave way to plain forms, while settlements occupied a wider range of places, including island interiors. A 2018 study argues that local ceramic production had ceased by about 2350 calibrated years before 1950, approximately 400 BCE. That estimate falls after this dossier’s 500 BCE endpoint. It marks a proposed change in material practice, not the disappearance of islanders or a universal stage that every Pacific society had to follow.

deeperReading.title: An island sequence has overlapping uncertainties
deeperReading.text: The 2015 Tongan analysis combined different dated materials and modeled the principal island groups separately. Its estimates placed expansion beyond Tongatapu within succeeding generations, while the first-settlement ranges for Ha’apai and Vava’u overlapped. Limited Vava’u samples constrained the proposed order. A useful timeline therefore displays an attributed model and uncertainty, rather than turning three named islands into an exact recovered itinerary for one crew.

deeperReading.title: Pottery and language answer related questions differently
deeperReading.text: Pawley argues for connections between Lapita archaeology and Oceanic language history through distributions, shared linguistic innovations and material terminology. He also notes that pottery could enter communities speaking other languages. A sherd does not record its maker’s speech. Keep the linguistic argument visible as a reconstruction, rather than use a decorative style as an ethnic badge or an automatic identification of every person who handled it.

subjects.question: Could people build a monumental place without depending on crop agriculture?
subjects.summary: Poverty Point’s American Indian builders joined monumental earthmoving with the continuing work of obtaining food, making tools and maintaining shared space. Local soil became both building material and shaped heating objects. The surviving landscape and small objects explain different parts of that work; neither supplies a complete political system or one construction date.

sections.title: A raised place beside useful lowlands
sections.text: People built the complex on Macon Ridge above nearby floodplain environments. Wetlands, woods and rivers offered different foods and materials, while the elevated ground supported settlement. The NPS bounds the main residential and ceremonial earthworks around 1700–1100 BCE. This is the history of a selected place, not the lifespan of an Indigenous people or every site grouped under the archaeological name Poverty Point.

sections.title: Moving earth required a sequence of tasks
sections.text: The state account describes builders preparing the ground for Mound B, adding layers and finally covering its surface. Such work involved obtaining, carrying and placing soil, with decisions about where each addition belonged. Mound A had a peak, platform and connecting ramp with a different sequence. A finished outline gathers these histories into one view; it does not show that every part was made together or reveal exactly how workers were recruited.

sections.title: Open space also had to be maintained
sections.text: The central plaza was built and cared for, rather than simply left empty between the ridges. People filled low spots and checked spreading gullies. Buried postholes record repeated setting of large wooden posts. These observations connect gathering space with recurring physical work. A modern LiDAR terrain model shows surviving surface forms; excavated deposits help establish changes that no overhead view can date alone.

Hunting, fishing and gathered plants supplied food without the crop dependence often assumed necessary for monumental building. Charred plant remains and surviving bones support that account, while poor bone preservation limits a complete menu. Preparing and sharing meals belonged alongside earthmoving in community life.

packs.title: Networks, resources and disruption
packs.question: How did regional societies interact, depend on resources and respond to disruption?
packs.orientation: Copper, tin, pottery, food and stories moved through particular networks. Communities also depended on landscapes, institutions and skilled work. Around 1200 BCE some eastern Mediterranean political centers changed dramatically. That regional investigation belongs beside other histories, with evidence for both disruption and continuity.
packs.geography: The main network case lies in Anatolia and the eastern Mediterranean. Move separately to the Nile, China, Mesoamerica and island Oceania. Earlier Caral and Dholavira contexts remain accessible where their occupation ranges overlap this window. Poverty Point adds a separate Lower Mississippi Valley investigation of earthworks, food and materials.
packs.limits: This chapter is selective. It does not establish one universal Bronze Age, a single cause of political change, or a global event in one exact year. European, inland South Asian and African regions beyond the selected Nile case need fuller accounts.

Americas.reason: Olmec and Poverty Point now have layered accounts, distinct phased contexts, geographic locators and material/source interpretation. These selected communities do not complete Gulf Coast, Lower Mississippi or wider American histories.

Africa.reason: Kerma-Egypt exchange and craft evidence; other African regions require separate histories.

Europe.reason: A sourced reference compares selected Aegean centres and British farms. There is not yet a standalone European dossier in this chapter; Uluburun remains a separately dated cargo comparison in West/Central Asia.

West/Central Asia.reason: Expanded Hattusha and Uluburun accounts distinguish capital phases, Gordion drought proxy, wreck association and contested tin provenance. These do not supply a full eastern Mediterranean or inland Asian reference history.

South Asia.reason: Dholavira’s later occupation provides an overlap with C1; it is not a full account of regional change after urban transitions.

East Asia.reason: Expanded Shang account separates the conventional period, Yin Xu late capital, ritual/casting practice and object-specific attribution. Household and wider regional coverage remain limited; no shared Anatolian collapse is inferred.

Southeast Asia/Oceania.reason: Lapita now joins pottery-making, provisioning and source-qualified island sequences, with a modern cast, original action guide and a correctly wrapped regional locator. Archaeological and linguistic reconstruction stay distinct; this is not a complete Pacific reference framework.

interval.note: Rounded orientation for the Phase 3 sequence, not proof of cultivation in every field in every intervening year. The published early range is 4350–3980 calibrated years before 1950 (about 2400–2030 BCE); the late range is 2700–2400 (about 750–450 BCE). This is a highland New Guinea setting, not a history of all Southeast Asia or Oceania.

contexts.summary: At Kuk in the upper Wahgi Valley, buried ditch networks show people altering wet ground for cultivation. Archaeologists distinguish early and later drainage episodes and compare Kuk with other highland sites. Draining soil could make land usable, but the surviving cuts do not name the workers, settle their land rights or reveal every crop. This agricultural history should be read alongside, rather than absorbed into, the later island settlements associated with Lapita pottery.

phases.title: Early Phase 3: a dated range
phases.text: The early ditch-network range is approximately 2400–2030 BCE. The opening year is a rounded edge of that range, not a known day when ditch digging began.

phases.title: Later drainage evidence
phases.text: The table places a later subphase around 750–450 BCE. The interval between the published subphases must not become a fabricated continuous list of annual events.

phases.title: An archaeological boundary, not the end of a people
phases.text: The selected late range ends here. The authors distinguish later phases and warn that other sites lack enough evidence to establish the same pattern of abandonment. Changing a field system does not by itself establish the disappearance of a community.

comparisons.question: How do cargo and ritual objects reveal different stages of skilled work?
What can a capital and a shipwreck tell us about changing networks?
How did different uses of clay connect skilled work with social or practical needs?
How can material observations and dated contexts distinguish a making technique, a practical use and a proposed connection?

orientations.title: Earthwork communities in different American landscapes
orientations.question: Does a large building project tell us how people obtained food or organized work?

summary.title: Supe, the Gulf Coast and the lower Mississippi
summary.text: Caral’s later building history, San Lorenzo’s constructed landscape and Poverty Point’s earthworks belong to different places and sequences. Large public spaces make collective work visible. They do not require us to assume one farming system, one political structure or contact among all three communities.

sections.title: Provisioning does not have one recipe
sections.text: Poverty Point’s hunter-fisher-gatherer communities used varied local foods while obtaining materials from farther away. In the Gulf Coast account, pottery and earth building accompany a different environmental and social history. Monument size alone cannot tell us whether every builder farmed, how food was distributed, or whether all work was compulsory.

citations.locator: San Lorenzo: pottery and monumental landscape

sections.title: A place changes without every community ending
sections.text: Caral’s broad development frame ends before 1200 BCE. Poverty Point’s main complex belongs to about 1700–1100 BCE, while San Lorenzo and later La Venta have separately described peaks. The appearance of a new prominent centre should not be read as the disappearance of all people or craft production at the earlier one.

citations.locator: After about 900 B.C.; later production at other centres

orientations.perspectives: Earthmoving and food remains bring builders and provisioners into view, but most individual arrangements of work are unrecovered. Museum labels describe evidence categories, not a single American people.
orientations.scope: Three selected settings, not a uniform American sequence. The old Caral record is a comparison across time, not a settlement extended into the 1200 BCE snapshot.

activity.prompt: A visitor says that large earthworks prove every community grew the same crops. Use one food record and one dated site to revise that claim.
activity.response: Use Poverty Point’s hunter-fisher-gatherer food evidence to separate subsistence from monument size. Then identify a particular site and date range; similar earthworks alone do not establish the same food system or contact.

snapshots.text: Around 1200 BCE, Poverty Point and San Lorenzo provide distinct settlement settings. Caral’s retained development range has already ended. Compare the earthworks and evidence of provisioning without placing all three at one simultaneous peak.

orientations.title: Kerma and the Nile: goods, institutions and changing control
orientations.question: How can exchange and political domination leave different evidence?

summary.title: A Nubian city and its northern neighbours
summary.text: Kerma’s craft production and imported burial goods reveal both local skill and exchange with Egypt. Relations also included conflict and diplomacy. The selected beaker makes ceramic work visible; it cannot stand for every household or for the full history of Nile politics.

sections.title: Making goods and moving goods are different tasks
sections.text: The project identifies institutions, walls and tombs in successive Kerma phases. Imported objects in tombs show the movement and selective use of goods. They do not name every producer, trader or carrier, and elite burial equipment does not measure ordinary household access.

citations.locator: Key Events: imports and local burial equipment

sections.title: The 1200 BCE setting comes after Kerma’s kingdom
sections.text: The museum places Upper Nubia under Egyptian control within a broad 1500–1070 BCE frame. It describes new settlements, temples and administration, including Napata near Jebel Barkal. This later institutional setting must be distinguished from Kerma’s earlier urban kingdom and the still earlier manufacture of the selected beaker.

citations.locator: Upper Nubia timeline; Key Events c1550–1070 BCE

orientations.perspectives: Tombs privilege selected elites; temples and administrative labels privilege institutions. Potters and other workers are visible through objects, without a complete record of their own accounts.
orientations.scope: Selected Nile and Nubian settings, not all African communities. Differing project and museum Kerma endpoints remain in the linked dossier; no exact universal conquest year is imposed.

activity.prompt: Distinguish what an imported burial object shows from what an administrative chronology shows. Why is the beaker not a 1200 BCE object?
activity.response: An import supports movement and burial use of a good; the chronology describes a broader political arrangement. The beaker has its own earlier catalogue range, so it is a comparison rather than a contemporary object.

snapshots.text: The selected Nile setting around 1200 BCE is Egyptian administration in Nubia, including temple and settlement development. Kerma’s earlier kingdom and the beaker remain earlier readings. Political control did not make every local person, craft or experience identical.

citations.locator: Upper Nubia: c1500–1070 BCE; Key Events c1550–1070 BCE

orientations.title: Palaces, workshops and farms across Bronze Age Europe
orientations.question: Whose work becomes visible when we look beyond a palace?

summary.title: Crete, mainland Greece and Britain
summary.text: Cretan centres such as Knossos and Phaistos concentrated goods, craft activity and record keeping. Mainland Greek centres provide later workshop and administrative evidence. British farms and fields offer a different settlement pattern within a longer Bronze Age frame.

sections.title: Records make some labour easier to see
sections.text: Clay records and specialized production show how some Aegean institutions organized resources. Britain’s round houses and field divisions instead draw attention to cultivation and household space. Different surviving evidence changes the questions we can answer; a place without palace records is not a place without skilled organization.

sections.title: Change was not synchronized
sections.text: The Cretan destruction horizon around 1450 BCE precedes the late-thirteenth-century destructions described for mainland centres. Britain’s broad Bronze Age sequence continues beyond both. The Uluburun cargo offers a comparison for circulating materials, not a proven route linking each of these selected places.

orientations.perspectives: Institutional accounts favour the categories their record keepers needed. Farms and workshops expose other practical tasks, without supplying every worker’s voice or status.
orientations.scope: Selected contrasting settings, not one European government or a common collapse. Uluburun is a cross-regional reading destination; no European origin or destination is assigned to its voyage.

activity.prompt: Choose a palace record and a field boundary as evidence. What work might each reveal, and why can neither prove one Europe-wide collapse?
activity.response: A record can identify institutional goods or labour categories; a field boundary can show organization of land. Each needs its own place and date. Neither extends a local destruction horizon to all European communities.

snapshots.text: Around 1200 BCE, the mainland Greek account describes destruction and declining palace institutions. British farming landscapes belong to a different, longer sequence. This comparison shows uneven change; it does not establish one event or cause across Europe.

orientations.title: Hattusha and Uluburun: institutions on land and cargo at sea
orientations.question: How can a city and a shipwreck reveal different kinds of organization?

summary.title: A capital and a cargo assemblage
summary.text: Hattusha’s palace, temples and archives reveal institutions within an Anatolian capital. The Uluburun wreck preserves a dated cargo off the southern coast of Anatolia. A city’s accumulated buildings and a ship’s lost load are different kinds of evidence, even when they belong within overlapping broad histories.

citations.locator: Project overview: capital and cult centre

sections.title: A cargo is not a complete trade network
sections.text: The wreck’s varied goods support questions about supply, loading and maritime exchange. They do not recover every port visited, the identity of all people aboard or a single merchant’s itinerary. Hattusha’s institutional evidence cannot fill those missing details merely because both places belong in an eastern Mediterranean inquiry.

sections.title: An institutional ending is not every resident’s ending
sections.text: The DAI overview frames Hattusha’s capital history approximately from 1650 to 1180 BCE and also describes later occupation. Composite city plans gather different phases. Around 1200 BCE, the broad capital frame is relevant; a precise citywide destruction date or a single cause cannot be inferred from that range.

orientations.perspectives: Palace records favour institutional concerns, while a wreck records a loss. Neither gives an ordinary household census or a full account from the people who moved the goods.
orientations.scope: Anatolian and maritime settings, not all West or Central Asia. The disputed drought/collapse causal claim is not used to fill this orientation; cargo origins and routes retain the dossier’s qualifications.

activity.prompt: A cargo contains materials from different regions. What does that support, and what additional evidence would be needed to draw a ship’s route?
activity.response: It supports circulation and assembly of goods. A route needs evidence for particular ports and voyage stages; a material’s origin alone cannot show each intermediate stop or identify the crew.

snapshots.text: Around 1200 BCE lies near the end of Hattusha’s broad capital-era frame. Its buildings represent multiple phases. Uluburun’s earlier cargo provides a separate exchange comparison, not a shipwreck dated to this selected year or proof of one cause of political change.

orientations.title: After major Indus cities: different settlement histories
orientations.question: How can we follow change without extending an earlier city’s lifespan?

summary.title: Dholavira and Bhagwanpura
summary.text: Dholavira’s changing urban layout belongs to a long occupation ending before this chapter’s 1200 BCE snapshot. Bhagwanpura, in the Kurukshetra district, supplies a separately dated village sequence. Reading the two together shifts attention from a single urban ending to differently situated communities.

sections.title: Pottery changes within an occupied place
sections.text: Kenoyer summarizes Bhagwanpura’s Late Harappan phase as 1700–1300 BCE and its Painted Grey Ware phase as 1400–1000 BCE. Some layers contain both pottery traditions. Their overlap supports investigation of local change and interaction rather than a simple empty interval between two named cultures.

citations.locator: Printed p43: chronology and mixed layers

sections.title: A material label does not identify a language
sections.text: The chapter describes changing pottery and differently shaped houses. It also cautions that pottery cannot determine the inhabitants’ language or religion. Earlier urban water systems at Dholavira remain a useful comparison for practical organization, but they cannot be assigned to Bhagwanpura or carried forward to 1200 BCE.

citations.locator: Printed p43: houses and limits of linguistic/religious identification

orientations.perspectives: Settlement remains expose household activities without supplying individual testimony. Archaeological classifications are not direct statements of how inhabitants named themselves.
orientations.scope: Two separately dated settings. Bhagwanpura’s dates follow the cited scholarly synthesis of the excavation; the entire excavation report has not been reviewed. Textual epic identification and racial interpretations are not adopted.

activity.prompt: Why can mixed pottery in a layer support a question about interaction without proving that everyone spoke the same language?
activity.response: The layer associates material traditions in a particular context. Speech and religious identity require different evidence. Also retain the possibility that deposit formation affects associations rather than assigning each pot to a distinct ethnic group.

snapshots.text: Around 1200 BCE falls within the cited 1400–1000 BCE Bhagwanpura phase. It is a later village setting, separate from Dholavira’s earlier urban occupation. The phase range does not date every house or pottery change to this exact year.

orientations.title: Yin Xu: craft, divination and royal institutions
orientations.question: What do royal records reveal, and whose experience do they leave out?

summary.title: A focused late-Shang setting
summary.text: Yin Xu near Anyang contains palace and ancestral-shrine areas, tombs and evidence of specialized craft. Oracle-bone inscriptions preserve particular questions and divinatory practices. These records open a view into royal institutions; they do not represent all communities across East Asia.

sections.title: Objects and inscriptions answer different questions
sections.text: A bronze vessel can expose choices of form, casting and use in ritual settings. An oracle inscription records a different activity: posing and interpreting a divinatory question. The selected museum objects have their own catalogue attributions; neither should be assigned to a particular excavated tomb without provenance evidence.

sections.title: The late capital is not the entire dynasty
sections.text: UNESCO dates Yin Xu’s late-capital frame to about 1300–1046 BCE. The broader Shang convention starts earlier. A change in dynasty around 1046 BCE should therefore be kept apart from transformations around 1200 BCE in distant Anatolia and the Aegean.

orientations.perspectives: Royal tombs and divination records favour court priorities. The labour of makers is visible through production, while ordinary residents’ own narratives remain much harder to recover.
orientations.scope: A justified local focus: shrine, burial and craft contexts at one late capital let us compare evidence types closely. This does not claim continuous coverage of every East Asian region or dynasty.

activity.prompt: Compare what a vessel’s manufacture and an inscribed question can tell you. Name one thing neither establishes about an ordinary family.
activity.response: Manufacture can reveal materials and skilled production; an inscription can reveal a recorded institutional concern. Neither alone establishes an ordinary family’s diet, political choices or access to those objects.

snapshots.text: Around 1200 BCE lies within Yin Xu’s late-Shang capital frame. Palace, shrine, tomb and divination evidence offer related but distinct views of institutions. The later Shang–Zhou transition is not moved back to this snapshot date.

orientations.title: Kuk, An Sơn and Lapita: sequences across land and sea
orientations.question: Why must farming, burial and island-settlement evidence keep separate dates?

summary.title: Three independent archaeological settings
summary.text: Kuk’s highland cultivation history, An Sơn’s mainland settlement and burial sequence, and Lapita pottery in island communities preserve different activities. Bringing them together broadens the regional view without making them stages of one migration or one economy.

sections.title: Local deposits record different work
sections.text: Kuk’s ditch networks concern water control. At An Sơn, occupation layers and later burials require separate dating. Pottery in Lapita settings can instead help investigate manufacture and circulation among island communities. Similar broad dates do not demonstrate that people at all three places followed the same farming or settlement practices.

sections.title: Island sequences cannot be backdated as a group
sections.text: The institutional account places Lapita emergence in the Bismarcks around 1500 BCE and a broad movement toward Remote Oceania around 1100–800 BCE. Particular Tongan sites have their own modeled dates. The earlier part of this chapter must not be filled with later Tongan settlement evidence.

orientations.perspectives: Archaeological evidence records actions through deposits and objects. It does not recover the identities of every cultivator, potter or voyager, and modern descendant communities are not interchangeable.
orientations.scope: Selected highland, mainland and island histories. Overlapping intervals are not an established route linking Kuk, An Sơn and every Lapita settlement.

activity.prompt: A map labels every Lapita island as settled by 1200 BCE. Explain how you would check and revise it.
activity.response: Compare each island’s dated settlement evidence with the regional overview. Do not use the early Bismarck frame to backdate Tonga or every other island. Mark unverified or later local sequences separately.

snapshots.text: Around 1200 BCE belongs within the broad Bismarck Lapita frame and near the later boundary of An Sơn’s selected burial sequence. Remote Oceanian settlement and individual Tongan sites require their own later or overlapping dates. This snapshot does not establish one contemporaneous chain of settled islands.

citations.locator: Bismarck emergence and Remote Oceania 1100–800 BCE
